lessons.title: Types of Extruders: Single-Screw vs. Twin-Screw
lessons.body:
Extruders are machines that cook, shape, and puff cereal dough in one continuous process. In Africa, small and medium enterprises (SMEs) often start with a single-screw extruder because it is cheaper and easier to maintain. A single-screw extruder has one rotating screw inside a barrel. It works well for simple puffed snacks and corn flakes, but it struggles with sticky or high-fat mixes. Typical single-screw models for SMEs cost between $2,000 and $8,000 and can produce 50â150 kg per hour. They need dry ingredients with less than 20% moisture and low fat (under 5%) to avoid slipping.

Twin-screw extruders have two intermeshing screws. They handle wet, sticky, and fatty recipes better, and they give more control over texture. They cost moreâ$15,000 to $50,000âbut can produce 100â500 kg per hour. Twin-screw extruders are ideal if you want to add local ingredients like moringa, groundnut flour, or insect protein. They also clean themselves better, reducing downtime between runs.

For a startup in Kenya or Nigeria, begin with a single-screw if your product is simple and dry. Upgrade to twin-screw when you need flexibility or higher output. Always check that the extruder motor matches your power supplyâmany African workshops have 220V single-phase, while larger extruders need 380V three-phase. Also, ensure spare parts like screws and dies are available locally or through importers. Training operators on the difference is critical: single-screw requires careful feed moisture control, while twin-screw allows more tolerance. Test your recipe on a rented machine before buying.

lessons.title: Extrusion Parameters: Temperature, Pressure, and Moisture
lessons.body:
Three settings control everything in extrusion: temperature, pressure, and moisture. Get them right, and you get consistent puffs. Get them wrong, and you get hard lumps or burnt cereal. Temperature is set in zones along the barrel. For corn flakes, typical zones are 60Â°C, 120Â°C, 160Â°C, and 180Â°C from feed to die. For puffed snacks, you might go higherâup to 200Â°C at the dieâto create steam that expands the product. Use a handheld infrared thermometer to check barrel temperatures if your machine lacks sensors. In Africa, ambient heat can affect cooling, so monitor closely.

Pressure builds up behind the die. Higher pressure means more expansion when the product exits. You control pressure by adjusting the die opening, screw speed, and feed rate. A pressure gauge on the die head is essential; typical values are 20â100 bar. If pressure is too low, the product wonât puff. Too high, and the machine may stall or back up.

Moisture is the most critical parameter. The feed should have 15â25% water by weight. Too dry, and the starch wonât gelatinize; too wet, and the product steams instead of puffs. Use a moisture meter (cost: $50â$150) to test your mix. Add water with a spray bottle or a peristaltic pump for consistency. In humid regions, pre-dry ingredients like maize or rice to 12% moisture before mixing. Always run a small test batch before full production. Record settings for each recipeâthis becomes your standard operating procedure.

lessons.title: Die Design and Product Shaping
lessons.body:
The die is the metal plate at the end of the extruder that shapes the product. It determines whether you make round puffs, stars, flakes, or tubes. Dies are made from hardened stainless steel to resist wear. A basic die for puffed snacks costs $200â$500; custom shapes can cost $1,000 or more. In Africa, local machining shops can sometimes replicate simple dies if you provide a sample, but precision matters for consistent expansion.

Die design affects pressure and texture. A die with a long land (the straight channel) increases pressure, leading to more expansion. A short land gives less puff. For corn flakes, you want a flat die with multiple small slots to create thin ribbons that later flake. For puffed cereals, a round die with a 3â5 mm hole is common. The number of holes determines output: more holes mean higher throughput but lower pressure per hole.

When designing a die, consider the productâs final shape and density. If you want light, airy puffs, use a die with a 4 mm hole and a land length of 8â10 mm. For denser, crunchier pieces, use a 2 mm hole and longer land. Always test a new die with a small batch. Check for uneven flowâsome holes may clog if the die is not polished. Clean the die after every run with a brass brush and warm water. Never use steel tools that can scratch the surface. Keep spare dies on hand to avoid production delays.

lessons.title: Texturization and Expansion Control
lessons.body:
Texturization is how you control the crunch, chew, or melt of your cereal. Expansion is the puffing that happens when superheated water flashes into steam as the product exits the die. The key variables are temperature, moisture, and screw speed. Higher temperature and lower moisture give more expansion. For a light, crispy puff, aim for 180â200Â°C at the die and 15â18% feed moisture. For a denser, crunchy texture, drop the die temperature to 140â160Â°C and increase moisture to 20â22%.

Screw speed also matters. Faster screw speed (300â500 rpm) creates more shear, which raises temperature and pressure, leading to more expansion. Slower speed (100â200 rpm) gives less expansion and a denser product. In Africa, many SMEs use variable frequency drives (VFDs) to adjust screw speed easily. A VFD costs $150â$400 and can be retrofitted to most motors.

To control texturization, you can also add ingredients. Starch from maize, rice, or cassava expands well. Adding 5â10% sugar or salt reduces expansion because they disrupt the starch matrix. Fibre from bran or moringa increases density. Fats and oils (above 2%) reduce expansion and can cause slippage in single-screw extruders. Always run a test matrix: change one variable at a time and record results. Use a simple scale to measure bulk densityâthe weight of a fixed volume of product. Lower density means more expansion. Aim for 50â100 g per litre for puffed cereals, 200â300 g per litre for flakes.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Common Extrusion Issues
lessons.body:
Extrusion problems waste time and money. Here are common issues and fixes. If the product wonât puff, check moisture firstâit may be too high. Reduce water addition by 2â3% and increase die temperature by 10Â°C. If the product is too hard, increase moisture or lower die temperature. If itâs burnt, reduce temperature in the last barrel zone or increase screw speed to move material faster.

Surgingâuneven flowâoften comes from inconsistent feed. Use a volumetric feeder or a screw conveyor to keep feed steady. If the extruder stalls, the die may be clogged or the feed too wet. Stop, clean the die, and reduce moisture. For single-screw extruders, slippage happens when fat content is too high. Reduce fat to below 5% or switch to a twin-screw.

Wear and tear: screws and barrels wear out after 1,000â2,000 hours. Replace worn screws to maintain pressure. Listen for unusual noisesâthey indicate misalignment or bearing failure. Keep a maintenance log. In Africa, power fluctuations can damage motors. Use a voltage stabilizer ($100â$300) to protect your machine. Also, train operators to never put hands or tools into the extruder while running. Safety first. When troubleshooting, change one thing at a time and wait 5 minutes for the system to stabilize. Keep a notebook with settings and outcomes for each recipe.

lessons.title: Case Studies: Corn Flakes and Puffed Cereals
lessons.body:
Case Study 1: Corn Flakes in Kenya. A small factory in Nakuru uses a single-screw extruder to make corn flakes. Recipe: 80% maize flour, 10% sugar, 5% salt, 5% malt extract. Feed moisture is 18%. Barrel temperatures: 60Â°C, 120Â°C, 160Â°C, 180Â°C. Die: flat with 0.5 mm slots. Screw speed: 250 rpm. The extruded ribbons are dried to 3% moisture, then toasted at 200Â°C for 2 minutes. Output: 80 kg/hour. They sell 500g packs for $1.20. Key success: consistent maize supply from local farmers and a moisture meter to check every batch.

Case Study 2: Puffed Rice Snacks in Nigeria. A womenâs cooperative in Ibadan makes puffed rice snacks using a twin-screw extruder. Recipe: 90% rice flour, 5% cassava starch, 5% palm oil. Feed moisture: 16%. Die temperature: 190Â°C. Screw speed: 400 rpm. Die: round with 4 mm holes. The product puffs directly from the die and is dried at 80Â°C for 10 minutes. Output: 150 kg/hour. They add local spices like ginger and pepper after drying. Selling price: $0.50 per 100g pack. Key success: twin-screw handles the oil and gives uniform puffs. They use a solar dryer to reduce energy costs.

Lessons: Start with a simple recipe and reliable equipment. Test locally available ingredients. Keep records. Train staff on safety and maintenance. Both cases show that extrusion can be profitable in Africa with the right parameters and market focus.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Extrusion Technology for African Breakfast Cereal Production

Extrusion is the engine room of modern breakfast cereal manufacturing. For African processors â whether you are running a 150 kg/hr pilot line in Nairobi or a 1.5 t/hr plant in Lagos â the extruder converts cheap, locally available raw materials (maize, sorghum, millet, cassava, soybean, groundnut) into high-value, shelf-stable, ready-to-eat (RTE) products. This lesson is a working reference: parameters, dies, troubleshooting, and the numbers you need to make capital and operating decisions. It assumes you have read the other lessons in this module; here we consolidate the practical detail.

1. The Extruder at a Glance

A single-screw extruder is cheaper (typically 30â50% lower capex) and adequate for simple puffed snacks and flaked cereals where shear history is not critical. A twin-screw extruder (co-rotating, intermeshing) gives independent control of screw speed, barrel temperature, and feed moisture, handles sticky or high-fat African formulations (e.g., 15â20% groundnut or soybean flour), and is the standard for texturized soy protein and co-extruded cereals. The decision is business-first: if your product portfolio is narrow (one puffed maize line), single-screw wins on payback. If you intend to diversify into soy-fortified, high-protein, or filled products, twin-screw is the platform.

2. Key Extrusion Parameters â Working Ranges

Your product quality (expansion, texture, colour, nutrient retention) is a function of five interacting variables: feed moisture, barrel temperature profile, screw speed, feed rate, and die geometry. Table 1 gives practical starting ranges for African cereal formulations. Always run a Design of Experiments (DoE) with your specific raw material â sorghum and millet behave differently from maize because of their higher protein and lower starch swelling power.

Table 1: Practical extrusion parameter ranges for African cereal blends
Parameter Single-Screw Twin-Screw Effect on Product
Feed moisture (% wb)14â20%12â25%Higher moisture = lower expansion, denser texture, better for flakes
Barrel temp. zone 1 (Â°C)60â9050â90Pre-conditioning, starch hydration
Barrel temp. zone 2 (Â°C)110â150100â150Gelatinisation onset
Barrel temp. zone 3 (Â°C)150â180150â190Cook, melt, texturize
Screw speed (rpm)80â150200â500Higher speed = more shear, higher expansion, lower bulk density
Die pressure (bar)20â6030â100Controls flash-off and expansion ratio
Specific mechanical energy (SME, kWh/kg)0.05â0.120.08â0.20Key scale-up and energy cost metric
Expansion ratio (radial)2.5â4.03.0â5.5Directly drives bowl-fill and perceived value

Sources: Moscicki (2011), Extrusion-Cooking Techniques; FAO (2013), Small-scale Cereal Extrusion, Agricultural and Food Engineering Working Document; Riaz, M.N. (2000), Extruders in Food Applications, Technomic.

3. Die Design and Texturization

The die is where your product identity is created. A simple circular die gives puffed balls or collets; a slit die gives ribbons; a multi-hole die with a rotating cutter gives the familiar "O" or "star" shapes. For corn flakes you want low expansion and a dense, flaky pellet â so use a slit die, high moisture (18â22%), low screw speed, and a subsequent flaking roll. For puffed cereals you want high expansion â use a small-diameter die (2â3 mm), low moisture (13â15%), and high screw speed.

Texturization â the fibrous, meat-like structure used in soy-based breakfast protein â requires a long die land (L/D of 3â5) and a cooling die to align protein fibres. In Africa, this is the technology behind soy-fortified cereal chunks and "meat analogue" breakfast proteins. The business case is strong: locally extruded texturized soy can replace imported textured vegetable protein (TVP) at 40â60% lower landed cost.

Table 2: Die and product shaping reference
Product Die Type Moisture Target Expansion Post-Extrusion
Puffed maize ballsCircular, 2â3 mm13â15%3.5â5.0ÃDry, coat, pack
Corn flakesSlit, 1Ã10 mm18â22%1.2â1.8ÃFlake rolls, toast, dry
Sorghum/millet snackStar or O-ring14â16%2.5â3.5ÃDry, season, pack
Texturized soy (TVP)Long-land slit + cooling die25â35%1.0â1.5ÃDry, size-reduce
Cassavaâgroundnut RTECircular, 3â4 mm15â18%2.0â3.0ÃDry, oil/season coat

Sources: Riaz (2000); FAO (2013); IITA (2018), Cassava Processing Technologies for Africa.

â  SAFETY WARNING â HIGH-PRESSURE EXTRUSION

The extruder barrel operates at 150â190Â°C and 30â100 bar. Never open the die head, clamp, or sampling port while the machine is pressurised or hot. Steam flash-off at the die can cause severe burns. Always:

  • Lock out/tag out (LOTO) before any die change or cleaning.
  • Wear heat-resistant gloves, face shield, and apron.
  • Allow barrel to cool below 60Â°C and pressure to read zero before disassembly.
  • Never reach into the feed hopper while screws are turning.
  • Keep a dry powder extinguisher and first-aid burn kit within 5 m of the line.

4. Troubleshooting Common Extrusion Issues

Most African processors face the same five problems. Here is the diagnostic sequence:

  • Product won't puff / low expansion: Check moisture first (too high), then die temperature (too low), then screw speed (too low). Sorghum and millet need 5â10Â°C higher die temperature than maize because their starch gelatinises at a higher temperature.
  • Surge / uneven flow: Usually feed inconsistency. Install a volumetric or gravimetric feeder; for sticky African blends (cassava, plantain), use a twin-screw feeder with agitation.
  • Burning / dark specks: Barrel temperature too high or residence time too long. Reduce zone 3 by 10Â°C and increase feed rate. Check for dead spots behind the die.
  • Die blockage: Moisture too low or foreign material (stones, metal). Install a magnet and a 2 mm screen before the feed hopper. Clean die holes with a brass brush, never steel.
  • High energy cost per tonne: Calculate SME. If above 0.15 kWh/kg, reduce screw speed and increase die open area â this alone can cut energy cost by 20â30%.

5. Business-First Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Raw material specification: Test moisture, starch, protein, and fat of every incoming batch. Fat above 6% requires twin-screw or pre-de-oiling.
  2. Feeder calibration: Weigh 1 minute of feed output weekly. Inconsistent feed = inconsistent product = customer complaints.
  3. Temperature profile logged: Record zone 1/2/3 every 30 minutes. Keep a logbook â this is your scale-up and quality data.
  4. Die inspection: Check die wear (hole diameter) monthly. A 0.2 mm wear changes expansion and fill weight.
  5. SME and kWh/tonne tracked: Know your energy cost per kg. Benchmark: 0.10â0.15 kWh/kg for puffed cereals.
  6. Moisture of finished product: Target 3â5% for shelf stability. Verify with a moisture analyser, not by feel.
  7. Packaging barrier: Use metallised or high-barrier film. African humidity (60â90% RH) destroys poorly packed cereals in weeks.
  8. Preventive maintenance: Replace screws and barrels per manufacturer hours; keep spare die and cutter head on site to avoid 2-week import delays.

6. Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Small-scale Cereal Extrusion (Agricultural and Food Engineering Working Document)
  • FAO â Cereal Processing Technologies (free online)
  • IITA â Cassava Processing Technologies for Africa
  • USDA ARS â Extrusion Processing Review (open access)
  • FAO Open Knowledge â Extrusion and Cereal Processing Repository

Prepared for RISE AFRICA Skills â Breakfast Cereals Module. All parameter ranges are starting points; validate with your own raw materials and equipment. Business decisions should be based on your local cost structure, energy tariffs, and target market.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of a twin-screw extruder over a single-screw extruder?
options: B) It handles sticky and high-fat mixes better
quiz.explanation: Twin-screw extruders can process wet, sticky, and fatty recipes that single-screw extruders cannot handle well.

quiz.q: Which moisture range is typical for feed in cereal extrusion?
quiz.explanation: Feed moisture of 15â25% allows proper starch gelatinization and expansion.

quiz.q: What does the die land length affect?
quiz.explanation: A longer land increases pressure, leading to more expansion of the product.

quiz.q: Which parameter most directly controls puffing?
quiz.explanation: Temperature and moisture determine how much steam flashes off, causing expansion.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of surging in extrusion?
quiz.explanation: Uneven feeding causes fluctuations in flow and pressure, leading to surging.

quiz.q: In the corn flakes case study, what was the final toasting temperature?
quiz.explanation: The case study states toasting at 200Â°C for 2 minutes.

quiz.q: Which ingredient reduces expansion in extrusion?
quiz.explanation: Sugar disrupts the starch matrix, reducing expansion.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost range for a single-screw extruder for SMEs?
quiz.explanation: Single-screw extruders for small enterprises typically cost between $2,000 and $8,000.

quiz.q: What does a VFD do on an extruder?
quiz.explanation: A variable frequency drive (VFD) allows easy adjustment of screw speed.

quiz.q: What is bulk density a measure of?
quiz.explanation: Bulk density indicates how much the product expanded; lower density means more expansion.

quiz.q: Which safety practice is essential when operating an extruder?
options: B) Never put hands or tools inside while running
C) Always run at maximum speed
D) Use water to cool the motor
quiz.explanation: Putting hands or tools into a running extruder can cause severe injury.

quiz.q: What is a sign of worn screws in an extruder?
quiz.explanation: Worn screws cannot generate enough pressure, leading to poor expansion.

quiz.q: In the puffed rice case study, what type of extruder was used?
quiz.explanation: The case study specifies a twin-screw extruder for puffed rice snacks.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a die with multiple holes?
options: A) To increase pressure per hole
quiz.explanation: More holes allow more product to exit at once, increasing throughput.

quiz.q: Which factor can cause slippage in a single-screw extruder?
quiz.explanation: Fat acts as a lubricant and can cause the screw to slip, reducing pumping efficiency.

quiz.q: What is a recommended moisture level for feed to make light, crispy puffs?
quiz.explanation: Lower moisture (15â18%) with high temperature gives more expansion and a lighter texture.

quiz.q: What should you do first when troubleshooting a non-puffing product?
quiz.explanation: Moisture is the most common cause; reducing it often solves the problem.

quiz.q: How often should screws and barrels be replaced?
quiz.explanation: Wear parts typically last 1,000â2,000 hours depending on use and maintenance.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using a voltage stabilizer with an extruder?
options: B) Protects motor from power fluctuations
quiz.explanation: Voltage stabilizers prevent damage from voltage spikes or sags, common in some areas.

quiz.q: Which ingredient can be added to increase fibre content in extruded snacks?
quiz.explanation: Moringa is a fibre-rich local ingredient that can be added to boost nutrition.

quiz.q: What is the typical pressure range in a cereal extruder?
quiz.explanation: Most cereal extruders operate between 20 and 100 bar at the die.

quiz.q: Why is record-keeping important in extrusion?
quiz.explanation: Recording settings and outcomes allows you to repeat good results and troubleshoot faster.

quiz.q: What is the main function of the die?
quiz.explanation: The die shapes the extruded product as it exits the machine.

quiz.q: Which local ingredient is commonly used in African extruded snacks?
quiz.explanation: Cassava is widely available in Africa and can be used in extrusion recipes.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a clogged die?
quiz.explanation: A clogged die restricts flow, causing pressure to spike and the extruder to stall.

quiz.q: How can you reduce energy costs in extrusion drying?
quiz.explanation: Solar dryers are a low-cost, sustainable option for drying extruded products.

quiz.q: What is the recommended fat content for single-screw extrusion?
quiz.explanation: High fat causes slippage; keep fat below 5% for single-screw extruders.

quiz.q: Which parameter is adjusted by changing the die opening?
quiz.explanation: A smaller die opening increases pressure, while a larger opening reduces it.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of burnt product in extrusion?
quiz.explanation: Excessive temperature in the barrel or die can scorch the product.

quiz.q: In the corn flakes case study, what was the output per hour?
quiz.explanation: The case study states an output of 80 kg/hour for corn flakes.
